To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the size of the microspores of heterosporous species of the lycophyte genus Selaginella tends to decrease with increasing leaf area index and net primary productivity of the habitat, whereas the size of the megaspores tends to increase with leaf area index, but there is a significant interaction with net primary productivity, such that in open habitats, species with smaller megasporangia are favored.
microspore and, to a lesser extent, megaspore size vary in a way that suggests that they are adapted to the light environment and the growth potential of habitats.
microspores are larger in habitats with low foliage cover and high growth rates, and that megaspores are larger in high‐density habitats with low growth rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the adaptive value of the heterospermous reproductive system of the lycophyte genus Selaginella and the ecological factors that may have led to its evolution.
the adaptive significance of micro- and megaspore sizes in Selaginella species.
understanding the functional ecology of heterospory in the lycophyte genus Selaginella, which has a wide geographical distribution and a diversity of microspore sizes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adaptive value of heterosporous reproduction is a function of habitat LAI and habitat NPP.
microspore size is related to microhabitat and megaspore to habitat characteristics.

the evolution of heterospory is a result of the increasing height of vegetation and the increasing density of the vegetative canopy, which led to the need to increase the dispersal ability of microspores.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
microspore size is correlated with the ability to disperse and germinate in open habitats, and that megaspore size is correlated to establishment ability in shaded habitats.

heterospory is a complex adaptation that evolved to cope with the increasing density and height of the Devonian vegetative canopy, but that the specific adaptations of microspores and megaspores have changed over the last ~350 million years.
microspore size is correlated with LAI and Npp, and megaspore sizes are correlated with NPP, but there is a strong interaction between the two variables.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adaptive value of heterosporous traits can be understood only in the context of a species’ entire life cycle, and that the adaptive value may vary across different environmental conditions.
heterospory can be a highly adaptive trait, but its adaptive value varies with the ecological context in which it occurs.
heterospory is not a single‐function innovation but instead a complex of traits that are adaptive in different ways in different environments.
